title: De Iudaeorum Vetustate sive Contra Apionem
author: Josephus
source: Translated by Claude from tlg0526.tlg003.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Inchoabo autem primitus a litteris Aegyptiorum, quas non arbitrantur commendare quae nostra sunt. Manethon itaque genere uir Aegyptiorum, Graeca disciplina participatus, sicut palam est, scripsit enim uoce Helladica, paternae regionis historiam ex sacris, sicuti ait ipse, interpretatus libris, frequenter arguit Herodotum in Aegyptiacis ignoratione mentitum.
passages.english: I shall begin first with the writings of the Egyptians, who are not thought to commend what is ours. Manetho, then, a man Egyptian by birth but sharing in Greek learning, as is evident (for he wrote in the Hellenic tongue), having translated the history of his ancestral country from the sacred books, as he himself says, frequently convicts Herodotus of having told falsehoods about Egyptian matters through ignorance.

passages.original: refert itaque in primo de Pythagora libro, quia Pythagoras uno confabulatorum suorum defuncto, nomine Calciphonte genere Crotoniate, illius animam dicebat secum degere die noctuque et quia praeciperet, ut non transiret de loco, unde asinus onus portaret, et ab aqua faeculenta semet ipsum abstineret et ab omni blasphemia recederet.
passages.english: He relates, then, in the first book on Pythagoras, that Pythagoras, when one of his companions had died, Calliphon by name, a Crotoniate by birth, used to say that the man's soul spent day and night with him; and that he enjoined that one should not pass over a place where an ass had carried a load, and should abstain from muddy water, and keep away from all blasphemy.
passages.notes: 'Calciphonte' is presumably Calliphon (the Greek has Kalliphōn). The author referred to ('he') is Hermippus in Josephus' Greek; the subject is not named in this passage.

passages.original: fuit autem etiam per ciuitates non ignota olim gens nostra, et multae nationes ad quas transiit etiam zelum eius habuerunt. quod manifestat Theophrastus in his, quae scripsit de legibus.
passages.english: Our nation, moreover, was once not unknown among the cities either, and many peoples to whom it passed over even held it in emulation. Theophrastus makes this plain in what he wrote on laws.
passages.notes: 'zelum eius habuerunt' could mean either that they emulated its customs or were zealous for it.

passages.original: CIearchus enim Aristotelis discipulus et ex peripato philosophorum nullo secundus in primo libro de somno dicit Aristotelem doctorem suum de quodam uiro Iudaeo ita referre, et ipsi Aristoteli eundem sermonem ascribit, quod ita conscriptum est: "Sed alia quidem longum est dicere.
passages.english: For Clearchus, a disciple of Aristotle and second to none of the philosophers of the Peripatos, says in the first book on sleep that his teacher Aristotle related the following about a certain Jewish man, and he attributes the account to Aristotle himself; it is written thus: "But it would take long to tell the other things.
passages.notes: 'CIearchus' is a scanning error for Clearchus.

passages.original: porro Aristoteles, secundum praecepta, inquit, rhetorica, eius genus primitus transeamus, ne reluctemur doctoribus praeceptorum. dic, inquit Hyperochides, ita si placet.
passages.english: Then Aristotle said: 'According to the rules of rhetoric, let us first go through his race, so as not to go against the teachers of the rules.' 'Speak so, if you please,' said Hyperochides.

passages.original: quod) habebat." Haec ait Aristoteles apud Clearchum et super haec multam atque mirabilem continentiam Iudaei uiri in cibis et castitatem narrans. licet autem uolentibus haec ex ipsius lectione cognoscere; ego enim refugio plus quam decet inserere.
passages.english: [...] which he had." This is what Aristotle says in Clearchus, and in addition he tells of the great and wonderful self-restraint of the Jewish man in his food, and his chastity. Those who wish may learn these things by reading [the book] itself; for I shrink from inserting more than is fitting.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence with a fragment ('quod) habebat'), the end of a quotation whose beginning is lost here.

passages.original: uerum Hecataeus quidem etiam librum conscripsit de nobis, Hieronymus autem nequaquam nostri historiam meminit, licet paene in ipsis locis nutritus esset: in tantum uoluntates hominum differebant. alio namque placuit studium habere memoria dignum, alio uero omnino circa ueritatem quaedam passio cernitur obscurasse.
passages.english: Hecataeus, indeed, even wrote a book about us, but Hieronymus nowhere mentions our history, although he was raised almost in those very places: so greatly did the inclinations of men differ. For one chose to pursue what was worthy of memory, while in the other some passion is seen to have quite obscured [his regard for] the truth.

passages.original: testantur, Polybius Megalopolita, Strabon Cappadox, Nicolaus Damascenus, Timagenes et Castor temporum conscriptor et Apollodorus; omnes dicunt pecuniis indigentem Antiochum. transgressum foedera Iudaeorum expoliasse templum auro argentoque plenum.
passages.english: [...] bear witness: Polybius of Megalopolis, Strabo the Cappadocian, Nicolaus of Damascus, Timagenes, and Castor the chronicler, and Apollodorus; all say that Antiochus, being in want of money, broke his treaties with the Jews and despoiled the temple, which was full of gold and silver.
passages.notes: The sentence begins mid-way; the subject list is preceded by lost context. The full stop after 'Antiochum' in the text appears misplaced and is ignored.

passages.original: caecus igitur fuit Apion, quando pro Aegyptiis nostras detractiones componens illos uidetur potius accusare, qui non solum utuntur sollemnitatibus, quas in nobis culpat iste, sed etiam alios circumcidi docent, sicuti dixit Herodotus.
passages.english: Apion, then, was blind, since in composing his slanders against us on behalf of the Egyptians he seems rather to accuse them, who not only practise the rites which he blames in us, but even taught others to be circumcised, as Herodotus said.

passages.original: quod Plato respiciens neque ullum quemquam poetarum dicit in republica esse suscipiendum et Homerum honorabiliter amouet fanum ei constituens et unguenta superfundens, ne rectam opinionem de deo fabulis forte destrueret.
passages.english: Having regard to this, Plato says that no poet at all is to be received in the republic, and he dismisses Homer with honour, setting up a shrine to him and pouring ointments over him, lest he should by chance destroy the right opinion about God with his myths.
passages.notes: 'fanum ei constituens' (setting up a shrine) differs from the Greek tradition, where Homer is crowned; translated as the Latin stands.
